plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 16: Chemistry of Benzene: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a reaction energy diagram set inside a pale blue rectangular panel, following benzene and bromine along two competing pathways. A tall arrow at the far left, shaded from pale yellow at the bottom to orange at the top, is labeled "Energy"; the horizontal axis beneath the panel reads "Reaction progress" and ends in a magenta arrow. Reactants sit on a dashed level at the left, drawn as a benzene hexagon, a plus sign, and "Br2" in magenta. A black curve climbs from that level to a high first maximum capped by a short dashed line, with a vertical double-headed arrow between maximum and reactant level labeled delta-G double-dagger. The curve drops into a trough, where a cationic intermediate is drawn as a partly unsaturated six-membered ring bearing an H and a magenta Br on the same carbon with a plus sign above it, then rises to a lower second maximum and falls to a dashed product level below the reactants, where bromobenzene plus "HBr" sit above the word "Substitution"; a small double-headed arrow labeled delta-G degrees spans the reactant-to-product gap. From the same trough a magenta curve branches upward over its own maximum and ends above the reactant level at a bracketed dibrominated ring labeled "Addition" and "(does not occur)". Placing both endpoints on one vertical energy scale is what carries the argument: the substitution branch finishes downhill while the addition branch finishes uphill.

interactionPlan.concept: Electrophilic bromination of benzene proceeds through a high first barrier to a carbocation intermediate, and then goes on to substitution — which restores aromaticity and ends downhill — rather than to addition, which destroys aromaticity and ends uphill.
elements: Pale blue rectangular panel enclosing the entire energy diagram
Vertical arrow at far left with a yellow-to-orange gradient, labeled 'Energy' in bold black rotated text
Horizontal axis caption beneath the panel: 'Reaction progress' followed by a magenta right-pointing arrow
Dashed horizontal reactant energy level on the left side
Reactant structures on that level: benzene hexagon (with inscribed circle or alternating double bonds), black plus sign, 'Br2' in magenta
Black substitution reaction curve: rises from reactant level to a tall first maximum, falls into a trough, rises to a lower second maximum, falls to a low product level
Short dashed horizontal tick capping the first maximum (TS1)
Vertical double-headed black arrow from first maximum down to reactant level, labeled 'ΔG‡'
Trough intermediate structure: cyclohexadienyl cation — six-membered ring with two double bonds, sp3 carbon bearing an H and a magenta Br, with a '+' sign above the ring
Second, lower maximum on the black curve (TS2)
Dashed horizontal product energy level below the reactant level
Small vertical double-headed arrow between reactant dashed level and product dashed level, labeled 'ΔG°'
Product structures on the low level: benzene ring with magenta 'Br' substituent, black plus sign, 'H' in black with 'Br' in magenta
Label 'Substitution' beneath the product structures
Magenta addition curve branching from the same trough, rising over its own maximum and ending on a plateau ABOVE the reactant level
Bracketed addition product: six-membered ring with one remaining double bond, two sp3 carbons each bearing an H (black) and a Br (magenta), enclosed in square brackets
Labels 'Addition' and bold magenta '(does not occur)' beneath the bracketed structure
Color legend cue: black = substitution pathway, magenta = bromine atoms / addition pathway

interactions.label: Walk the reaction coordinate
interactions.teaches: Electrophilic aromatic bromination is a two-step process: a slow, high-barrier attack on the electrophile gives a carbocation intermediate, which then loses H+ over a much smaller second barrier.

interactions.label: Fate of the intermediate
interactions.teaches: From the same intermediate, substitution descends below the reactants because aromaticity is regained, while addition climbs above them because aromatic stabilization is permanently lost — so only substitution occurs.

ΔG‡ measures the climb from reactants to the highest transition state (how fast), while ΔG° measures the net drop from reactants to products (how favorable) — two independent quantities on the same vertical scale.

demo_steps.title: Reactants on the baseline
demo_steps.narration: Benzene and Br2 sit on the left dashed level; everything else in the diagram is measured vertically against this line.

demo_steps.title: The big first barrier
demo_steps.narration: The black curve climbs steeply to the first transition state. Breaking benzene's aromaticity to attack Br+ costs a large ΔG‡, which is why bromination needs a FeBr3 catalyst.

demo_steps.title: The carbocation intermediate
demo_steps.narration: The curve drops into a real minimum: the cyclohexadienyl cation, with H and Br on the same sp3 carbon and a delocalized positive charge. It is a genuine, if fleeting, species — not a transition state.

demo_steps.title: Second, smaller barrier
demo_steps.narration: Loss of H+ from the sp3 carbon crosses a much lower maximum — this step is fast compared with the first.

demo_steps.title: Substitution ends downhill
demo_steps.narration: Bromobenzene plus HBr land below the reactant level: the aromatic ring is restored, so ΔG° is negative and the reaction is favorable.

demo_steps.title: The road not taken: addition
demo_steps.narration: Switch the branch and the magenta curve leaves the same intermediate but finishes ABOVE the reactants — the dibromide has no aromatic stabilization, so addition is uphill and does not occur.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Both pathways share the same intermediate, so the choice is decided entirely by where they end: substitution regains the ~150 kJ/mol of aromatic stabilization and finishes below the reactants, while addition sacrifices it permanently and finishes above them.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Wide pale-blue panel with a thin black border. Far left, outside the panel, a tall upward arrow filled with a pale-yellow-to-orange vertical gradient, labeled 'Energy' in bold rotated black text. Below the panel, centered, 'Reaction progress' followed by a magenta arrow pointing right. Inside: a smooth black curve starting on a left dashed level at mid-low height, rising to a tall peak near the left third (peak capped by a short dashed tick), dipping to a shallow trough in the middle, rising again to a second, noticeably lower peak, then plunging to a dashed product level near the bottom right — clearly below the reactant dashed level. A magenta curve branches out of the same trough, rises to its own intermediate-height maximum just right of the black second peak, and levels off on a plateau above the reactant dashed level on the right. Structures drawn as line-angle skeletons: plain benzene hexagon plus magenta 'Br2' at lower left; in the trough, a cyclohexadienyl cation (ring with two double bonds, one sp3 carbon carrying black H and magenta Br, a '+' above); at the bottom right, bromobenzene with magenta Br plus black 'H' and magenta 'Br', captioned 'Substitution'; at the upper right inside square brackets, a ring with one double bond and two adjacent sp3 carbons each bearing black H and magenta Br, captioned 'Addition' with bold magenta '(does not occur)'. Annotation arrows: a long vertical double-headed black arrow from the first peak's dashed tick down to the reactant dashed level labeled 'ΔG‡'; a short vertical double-headed arrow between the reactant dashed level and the product dashed level labeled 'ΔG°'. Highlighting convention: active stage marker is a filled dot on the curve plus a glow around the corresponding structure; the inactive branch dims to light gray; clicking an energy arrow thickens it and extends its two dashed reference levels fully across the panel.

authoredContext:
Why does the reaction of Br2 with benzene take a different course than its reaction with an alkene? The answer is straightforward. If addition occurred, the 150 kJ/mol stabilization energy of the aromatic ring would be lost and the overall reaction would be endergonic. When substitution occurs, though, the stability of the aromatic ring is retained and the reaction is exergonic. An energy diagram for the overall process is shown in the figure.

An energy diagram for the electrophilic bromination of benzene. Because the stability of the aromatic ring is retained, the overall process is exergonic.

Energy diagram shows curve exhibiting two peaks, with the first peak higher than second. A second curve originates from the trough of the first curve and ends higher in energy than the first curve.

interactions.teaches: From the same intermediate, substitution descends below the reactants because aromaticity is regained, while addition climbs above them because aromatic stabilization is permanently lost — so only substitution occurs.

ΔG‡ measures the climb from reactants to the highest transition state (how fast), while ΔG° measures the net drop from reactants to products (how favorable) — two independent quantities on the same vertical scale.

demo_steps.title: Reactants on the baseline
demo_steps.narration: Benzene and Br2 sit on the left dashed level; everything else in the diagram is measured vertically against this line.

demo_steps.title: The big first barrier
demo_steps.narration: The black curve climbs steeply to the first transition state. Breaking benzene's aromaticity to attack Br+ costs a large ΔG‡, which is why bromination needs a FeBr3 catalyst.

demo_steps.title: The carbocation intermediate
demo_steps.narration: The curve drops into a real minimum: the cyclohexadienyl cation, with H and Br on the same sp3 carbon and a delocalized positive charge. It is a genuine, if fleeting, species — not a transition state.

demo_steps.title: Second, smaller barrier
demo_steps.narration: Loss of H+ from the sp3 carbon crosses a much lower maximum — this step is fast compared with the first.

demo_steps.title: Substitution ends downhill
demo_steps.narration: Bromobenzene plus HBr land below the reactant level: the aromatic ring is restored, so ΔG° is negative and the reaction is favorable.

demo_steps.title: The road not taken: addition
demo_steps.narration: Switch the branch and the magenta curve leaves the same intermediate but finishes ABOVE the reactants — the dibromide has no aromatic stabilization, so addition is uphill and does not occur.

plan.keyInsight: Both pathways share the same intermediate, so the choice is decided entirely by where they end: substitution regains the ~150 kJ/mol of aromatic stabilization and finishes below the reactants, while addition sacrifices it permanently and finishes above them.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Wide pale-blue panel with a thin black border. Far left, outside the panel, a tall upward arrow filled with a pale-yellow-to-orange vertical gradient, labeled 'Energy' in bold rotated black text. Below the panel, centered, 'Reaction progress' followed by a magenta arrow pointing right. Inside: a smooth black curve starting on a left dashed level at mid-low height, rising to a tall peak near the left third (peak capped by a short dashed tick), dipping to a shallow trough in the middle, rising again to a second, noticeably lower peak, then plunging to a dashed product level near the bottom right — clearly below the reactant dashed level. A magenta curve branches out of the same trough, rises to its own intermediate-height maximum just right of the black second peak, and levels off on a plateau above the reactant dashed level on the right. Structures drawn as line-angle skeletons: plain benzene hexagon plus magenta 'Br2' at lower left; in the trough, a cyclohexadienyl cation (ring with two double bonds, one sp3 carbon carrying black H and magenta Br, a '+' above); at the bottom right, bromobenzene with magenta Br plus black 'H' and magenta 'Br', captioned 'Substitution'; at the upper right inside square brackets, a ring with one double bond and two adjacent sp3 carbons each bearing black H and magenta Br, captioned 'Addition' with bold magenta '(does not occur)'. Annotation arrows: a long vertical double-headed black arrow from the first peak's dashed tick down to the reactant dashed level labeled 'ΔG‡'; a short vertical double-headed arrow between the reactant dashed level and the product dashed level labeled 'ΔG°'. Highlighting convention: active stage marker is a filled dot on the curve plus a glow around the corresponding structure; the inactive branch dims to light gray; clicking an energy arrow thickens it and extends its two dashed reference levels fully across the panel.

discrepancies: The magenta addition curve in the source ends at a level ABOVE the reactant dashed line (higher energy than benzene + Br₂ — the whole point of the figure). In the generated figure the magenta branch terminates at y≈220, which is above the reactant level in screen coords but the reactant dashed line sits at y≈312, so the magenta endpoint is actually drawn higher on the page = higher energy — this is correct; however no dashed reference level or label marks the addition product level, weakening the visual comparison that the source implies via the bracketed structure's vertical placement.

Structure sizes/positions are noticeably compressed relative to the source: the reactant benzene ring, the cation, and the product ring are smaller and the cation structure sits closer to the curve, so the '+' charge label and H/Br bonds crowd the black curve (the source keeps them in clear open space).

The 'Addition (does not occur)' bracketed structure is rendered smaller and the bracket is tighter than the source, and the 'H' on the upper-left carbon is placed inside/above the ring rather than on a clean vertical bond as in the source.

ΔG‡ label is placed to the left of the arrow at mid-height, slightly overlapping the ascending black curve region; in the source it sits cleanly in the open area to the left of the vertical arrow with more clearance.

Minor: the source's short dashed tick at the top of the ΔG‡ arrow and the reactant/product dashed levels are present, but the gradient energy arrow tapers differently (source is a solid orange-to-cream arrow of similar proportion) — acceptable.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and well-annotated recreation of the bromination energy diagram with correct two-branch topology, chemical structures, ΔG‡/ΔG° arrows and rich, pedagogically sound interactions (6-step player, stage slider, branch toggle, energy-arrow comparison); main weaknesses are slightly cramped structure placement/scale and some label crowding near the cation and ΔG‡ arrow.
action_items: Enlarge the reactant benzene, cation, product and bracketed addition structures ~10–15% and nudge the cation group right/down so its '+' charge and H/Br labels clear the black curve, matching the source's generous spacing.
Reposition the ΔG‡ text further left/down so it never touches the ascending curve, and add the short dashed tick at the top of the ΔG‡ arrow exactly aligned with the TS1 apex as in the source.
Draw a faint dashed reference level at the addition-product endpoint (and optionally a labelled ΔG° for addition) so the 'ends above the reactants' conclusion is visually explicit.
Redraw the addition-product H on the upper-left carbon as an explicit vertical bond with the label outside the ring, and widen the square brackets to match the source proportions.
